existence-kalam-contingency: These are the two oldest arguments for God's existence still in serious use, and they answer different questions. The Kalam asks why there is a universe at all if it had a beginning: whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began, so the universe has a cause. The contingency argument sidesteps beginnings entirely and asks why anything exists that could just as easily not have. Neither delivers Christianity — at most they deliver something outside the universe that the universe depends on. That is a smaller conclusion than most people argue for, and it is the one worth defending.
existence-fine-tuning: Physics contains a set of numbers that are not derived from anything — the strength of gravity, the mass of an electron, the energy of empty space. Change several of them very slightly and no stars form, or no chemistry, or no universe that lasts long enough for anything to happen. The cosmological constant is the sharpest example: it sits at roughly one part in 10^120 of its natural value. The observation is not disputed; what it means is, and the standard alternative explanation is that vastly many universes exist and we necessarily find ourselves in a habitable one.
existence-moral-argument: The argument here is not that atheists cannot be good people — they obviously can be, and saying otherwise ends the conversation. It is narrower: that some moral facts feel discovered rather than invented. Torturing children for entertainment does not seem wrong because we decided it is; it seems to have been wrong before anyone said so. If that intuition is tracking something real, the question is what kind of universe contains facts of that sort. If it is not, the question is what we are doing when we condemn a genocide.
existence-argument-from-reason: This one is less familiar and harder to shake off. If your reasoning faculty was produced entirely by processes selecting for survival rather than for truth, there is a question about whether it can be trusted on questions far removed from survival — like ultimate metaphysics. Notably, the sharpest versions come from non-Christians: Thomas Nagel, an atheist philosopher, has pressed a version of it, and Darwin himself worried about it in a letter. It is a doubt aimed at a worldview from inside that worldview.
resurrection-minimal-facts: This is the argument's foundation, and its whole design is to avoid asking the other person to accept anything on your authority. Instead of arguing from the Bible as Scripture, it builds only on facts granted by the large majority of scholars in the field, including agnostics and atheists: that Jesus was crucified under Pilate, that his followers had experiences they took to be appearances of him alive, that Paul the persecutor changed sides after such an experience, that his skeptical brother James did too, and that the proclamation began immediately in Jerusalem. The argument is then simply: what explains all five?
resurrection-early-creed: The most common explanation for the resurrection story is that it grew over time — a legend accumulating across decades until it hardened into a Gospel. This case examines the one piece of evidence that makes that difficult. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul quotes a short formula he says he 'received' and passed on: that Christ died, was buried, rose, and appeared. The wording, structure and vocabulary mark it out as an existing creed he is repeating, and most scholars — including skeptical ones — date it to within about five years of the crucifixion.
resurrection-hallucination-hypotheses: If the disciples genuinely believed they saw Jesus alive, and there is broad scholarly agreement that they did, then the explanation everybody reaches for is that they were mistaken rather than lying. This case steelmans that seriously rather than dismissing it, because grief hallucinations are real, well documented, and common. The strain comes when you try to extend the explanation: hallucinations are typically individual rather than group events, and the two hardest cases are Paul, who was hostile, and James, who was skeptical — neither of whom was grieving a beloved teacher.
resurrection-willing-to-die: 'They died for it' is one of the most-repeated arguments in Christian conversation, and in its usual form it does not work — people die for false beliefs constantly, which any skeptic will point out immediately. This case rescues the narrow version that does work. The disciples were not believing someone else's testimony about an event they never saw; they were claiming to have eaten with a man they watched die. That is a claim about which they could not be honestly mistaken in the way a second-hand believer can. It rules out deliberate fraud, and nothing more.
manuscripts-nt-text: Every ancient book reaches us through hand-copies, and hand-copying introduces errors. For the New Testament there are around 5,800 Greek manuscripts plus many thousands in other languages — vastly more than for any other work of antiquity — and comparing them turns up something in the region of 400,000 differences. That number sounds devastating and gets quoted constantly. The reason it is so large is the reason the text is secure: more copies means more countable differences. This case walks through what those differences actually are.
manuscripts-dead-sea-scrolls: Before 1947, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts dated from around 1000 AD — a thousand-year gap between the copies we had and the events they described, and plenty of room to argue the text had drifted. Then a Bedouin shepherd found jars in a cave near the Dead Sea. The scrolls pushed the manuscript evidence back more than a millennium, and gave scholars a chance to run a controlled test: compare a copy from 100 BC against a copy from 1000 AD and see what a thousand years of hand-copying had done.
manuscripts-canon-formation: Popular retellings — The Da Vinci Code most famously — describe the Emperor Constantine convening the Council of Nicaea in 325 to vote on which books would be in the Bible and to suppress rival gospels. Almost none of that happened. This case sets out what actually did: a slow process of recognition by usage across the first three centuries, driven by whether a book was apostolic and whether the churches were already reading it, with a list from 367 AD that matches the New Testament you own.
archaeology-ot-corroboration: For much of the twentieth century a school of scholarship held that the early Israelite kings were essentially legendary — that David was to Israel what King Arthur is to Britain. Archaeology has been unusually unkind to that view. This case walks through the specific finds: a ninth-century BC stone inscription in which an enemy king boasts of defeating 'the House of David,' Hezekiah's water tunnel with its dedication inscription, and the Assyrian king Sennacherib's own account of besieging Jerusalem, which lines up strikingly with the biblical version.
archaeology-nt-corroboration: The New Testament makes a great many incidental claims about a real world — named officials, specific pools, particular titles for local rulers that changed from province to province. Those are checkable, and checkable details are how historians test whether a writer knew the world he was describing. This case collects the ones that have surfaced: an inscription naming Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judaea, an ornate bone-box bearing the name of the high priest Caiaphas, and the Pool of Siloam from John 9, uncovered during a sewer repair in 2004.
archaeology-quirinius-census: This case is here because a site that only prints its wins does not deserve to be believed. Luke dates Jesus's birth to a census under Quirinius, governor of Syria — but the census we know of took place in AD 6, roughly a decade after Herod the Great died, and Luke also places the birth in Herod's reign. That is a genuine difficulty. Several solutions have been proposed, none has become a consensus, and the honest thing is to say so out loud before anyone else does.
prophecy-tyre-babylon: Ezekiel 26 pronounces destruction on the Phoenician port of Tyre, and Isaiah and Jeremiah do the same for Babylon. Both are staples of prophecy sermons, and both are routinely overclaimed. The real history is more interesting and more complicated than the sermon version: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years without taking the island, Alexander later built a causeway out to it using the mainland rubble, and a town called Tyre exists today. This case sorts what the texts actually say from what gets said about them.
prophecy-daniel-dating: Daniel contains startlingly specific predictions about the sequence of empires and, in chapter 11, about the wars of the Greek successor kingdoms. The mainstream critical answer is that it was written after the fact, around 165 BC during the Maccabean crisis, which would make it history in the costume of prophecy. This case steelmans that dating properly — the arguments for it are real — and then asks what survives on either dating, which turns out to be more than most people on either side expect.
prophecy-isaiah53-psalm22: Any argument that a text predicted something invites the obvious reply: the text was written or edited afterwards. For Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 that reply can be tested and closed. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran contains the entire book, copied around 125 BC, and a Psalms fragment from the same region does the same job for Psalm 22. Whatever you conclude about the passages, they demonstrably existed before the events they are said to describe. Nobody added them.
objection-problem-of-evil: This is the reason most people give for not believing, and it deserves better than a quick answer. It comes in two forms that need to be kept apart. The logical form — that suffering is strictly incompatible with a good, all-powerful God — is now widely regarded as unsuccessful, including by atheist philosophers, largely because of the free-will defense. The evidential form is a different animal: not that suffering disproves God, but that the sheer amount and distribution of it counts as evidence against him. That version is live, serious and hard.
objection-divine-hiddenness: Most Christians have never heard this argument, and it is probably the strongest one in contemporary atheist philosophy after the problem of evil. J. L. Schellenberg's version runs: a perfectly loving God would want a relationship with every person open to one; a relationship requires believing the other party exists; yet there are people who are genuinely open and still do not believe. If that is true, something has to give. It is worth stating accurately before answering, because a Christian who can do that is rare.
objection-canaanite-conquest: The commands in Joshua and 1 Samuel to destroy the Canaanites and the Amalekites — including, in the text, women and children — are the hardest passages in the Bible to read, and no honest treatment makes them comfortable. This case lays out the four main approaches Christians actually take, including ones that disagree sharply with each other, and is clear that each of them costs something. Softening the text before reading it is the one move guaranteed to fail with a skeptic, who has usually read it already.
objection-who-made-god: 'If everything needs a cause, what caused God?' is the most common objection to the cosmological argument and it is asked in good faith far more often than Christians assume. The short answer is that the argument's premise was never 'everything needs a cause' but 'everything that *begins to exist* needs a cause' — so an eternal being is not an exception smuggled in but the thing the argument is reasoning toward. This case also notes where the objection still has real force.
objection-science-genesis: A great many conversations about God get diverted into arguments about the age of the earth and never come back. This case exists to say plainly that Christianity is not committed to a young earth: the church has held several readings of Genesis 1 for a very long time, including from Augustine in the fourth century, and a large share of Christians in the sciences hold none of the positions a skeptic is expecting. Choosing that hill means the actual claim — a man executed under Pilate and seen alive afterwards — never gets discussed.
objection-religion-wars: 'Religion causes most wars' is asserted constantly and is straightforwardly checkable. The standard reference work catalogues roughly 1,760 wars and classifies about 7% as religious in origin; the twentieth century's largest death tolls came from explicitly secular regimes. Those numbers are real. This case also insists on the second half, which most Christian responses skip: the Crusades, the Inquisition and the wars of religion happened, Christians did them, and a rebuttal that only cites statistics has not answered the person in front of you.
dontuse-banana-design: The banana argument — the fruit's shape and ridges as evidence of design — is probably the single most mocked moment in modern apologetics, and it is still repeated. This case explains why it fails in a way that is worth understanding rather than just avoiding: the modern banana is a human cultivar, selectively bred over centuries from a wild fruit full of hard seeds. It is a genuine argument for intelligent design, just not the kind intended. 'Just look at the trees' fails for a related reason.
dontuse-anti-evolution-science: Two claims in particular still circulate widely in churches: that there are no transitional fossils, and that the second law of thermodynamics makes evolution impossible. This case is blunt that both are false, and shows why the second is worse than the first — the second law applies to closed systems, and the earth receives energy from the sun continuously, which a skeptic with a high-school physics class behind them will point out. Using either tells your listener that you repeat things you have not checked.
dontuse-darwin-recanted: The story that Darwin renounced evolution on his deathbed and asked for the Gospel to be preached traces to a woman known as Lady Hope, who claimed to have visited him. Darwin's daughter Henrietta, who was present during his final illness, denied it flatly and in print. The story keeps circulating because it is satisfying. This case treats it as a test case in source-checking: the person you are talking to can disprove it on a phone in twenty seconds, and will then reasonably discount everything else you said.
dontuse-pascals-wager-opener: Pascal's wager — that betting on God is rational given what is at stake — is a genuinely interesting piece of philosophy, and it was never designed to do the job it is usually given. Pascal aimed it at someone already persuaded the odds were non-trivial and unable to move the final inch. Led with, it lands as an invitation to fake a belief for insurance purposes, which is both poor philosophy and poor theology, and it invites the obvious reply about all the other gods on offer.
dontuse-atheist-mind-reading: 'You know God exists and you're suppressing it.' 'You just want to keep sinning.' 'Atheism takes more faith than Christianity.' Each of these tells the person in front of you that you are addressing a stereotype rather than them, and each one ends the conversation while feeling, to the speaker, like a point scored. This case is about why they fail even when the underlying theology is defensible — a claim about someone's inner motives is not something you can know, and they can tell.
dontuse-all-twelve-martyred: 'All twelve apostles were tortured to death and not one recanted' is a sermon staple, and there is no ancient source that says it. The New Testament records one apostolic death; John is traditionally held to have died of old age; and the vivid traditions about the rest come from second-to-fourth-century romances that also feature talking animals. This case is graded from Sean McDowell's own research — an apologist who set out to defend this evidence and documented honestly how little of it can be established.
